questions.question: Which OOP concept best models the relationship between Piece and its subclasses (King, Queen, Rook, etc.)?
options: Composition
Inheritance with an abstract base class
Aggregation
Dependency injection
questions.explanation: Piece is an abstract class defining common attributes (color, position) and an abstract canMove method. Each piece type inherits from Piece and provides its own movement logic, making inheritance the natural fit.

questions.question: How is the chessboard typically represented in an object-oriented chess design?
options: A linked list of pieces
A 2D array of Cell objects, each optionally containing a Piece
A hash map from piece names to positions
A single string encoding all positions
questions.explanation: An 8x8 2D array of Cell objects provides O(1) access to any square. Each Cell holds its coordinates and an optional reference to a Piece. This makes move validation and board rendering straightforward.

questions.question: What three validation layers must a chess move pass before being executed?
options: Authentication, authorization, and logging
Piece geometry, path clearance, and king safety
Input parsing, formatting, and output
Network latency, bandwidth, and throughput
questions.explanation: First, the piece must be able to reach the target square geometrically. Second, the path must be clear of obstructing pieces (except for knights). Third, the resulting position must not leave the player's own king in check.

questions.question: How is check detected in a chess game?
options: By checking if the king is on the edge of the board
By iterating over all opponent pieces and checking if any can legally move to the king's square
By counting the number of pieces remaining
By checking if the king has moved more than three times
questions.explanation: Check is detected by examining every opponent piece and determining if any of them have a valid move targeting the king's current square. If at least one can, the king is in check.

questions.question: What conditions define checkmate?
options: The king is captured by an opponent piece
The king is in check and no legal move can remove the check
All pieces except the king have been captured
The king has not moved for ten consecutive turns
questions.explanation: Checkmate occurs when the king is in check and there is no legal move available: the king cannot move to a safe square, no friendly piece can block the attack, and no friendly piece can capture the attacking piece.

questions.question: Which design pattern is best suited for implementing undo/redo of chess moves?
options: Observer pattern
Command pattern
Singleton pattern
Factory pattern
questions.explanation: The Command pattern encapsulates each move as an object with execute() and undo() methods. This allows the game to maintain a history stack, enabling undo by calling the most recent command's undo method.

questions.question: What are the prerequisites for castling to be a legal move?
options: The king must be in check and needs to escape
Neither king nor rook has moved, no pieces between them, king does not pass through check
The rook must be adjacent to the king
Castling is allowed at any time as long as both pieces are alive
questions.explanation: Castling requires: (1) neither the king nor the chosen rook has previously moved, (2) no pieces stand between them, (3) the king is not currently in check, and (4) the king does not pass through or land on a square attacked by an opponent.

questions.question: What is stalemate and how does it differ from checkmate?
options: Stalemate means both players agree to a draw
Stalemate occurs when a player has no legal moves but is NOT in check, resulting in a draw
Stalemate is when only kings remain on the board
Stalemate occurs when the same position repeats twice
questions.explanation: Stalemate occurs when the player whose turn it is has no legal move available, but their king is NOT in check. Unlike checkmate which is a loss, stalemate results in a draw. This distinction is critical for game-ending logic.

questions.question: Why is the Knight the only piece that does not require path clearance validation?
options: Knights are too weak to be blocked
Knights jump over other pieces in an L-shape, so intervening pieces are irrelevant
Knights can only move one square at a time
Knights are always placed on the edge of the board
questions.explanation: The Knight moves in an L-shape (two squares in one direction, one in the perpendicular) and jumps over any pieces in between. Unlike Rooks, Bishops, and Queens, it does not slide along a path, so path obstruction does not apply.

questions.question: How would you efficiently detect threefold repetition (draw by repetition) in a chess game?
options: Compare the current board to every previous board state pixel by pixel
Hash each board position and store counts in a hash map, triggering draw when count reaches three
Store all moves in a list and check for repeated move sequences
It cannot be detected efficiently and must be claimed by a player
questions.explanation: Zobrist hashing assigns random bitstrings to each piece-square combination. XORing them together produces a unique hash for each board position. Storing these hashes in a map with occurrence counts allows O(1) detection of threefold repetition.
